keywords.term: Asleep surgery, Attentional outcomes, Awake brain surgery, High-grade glioma, Low-grade glioma, Oncological outcomes, Overall survival ANOVA, Analysis of Variance

div.p: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Patients with gliomas often experience neuropsychological deficits affecting their quality of life. Awake surgery (AwS) can reduce permanent cognitive deficits compared with asleep surgery (AsS), but it does not allow intraoperative mapping of all cognitive functions, including attention. Understanding how AwS and AsS affect attention is crucial, given its pivotal role in supporting various cognitive functions. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective analysis on 64 glioma patients treated with AwS or AsS. Attention was assessed with visual search tasks and Trail Making Test Part A before and 1 week and 1 month after surgery. Volumetric T1-weighted and T2/Fluid Attenuated Inversion Recovery MRI sequences before and after surgery were used to delineate the lesion and the surgical cavity. The extent of resection was calculated to determine supramaximal resection for both contrast-enhanced and non-contrast-enhanced tumor regions. RESULTS: There was a significant decrease in attentional scores 1 week after surgery, followed by a complete recovery. AwS was the only significant predictor of postoperative attentional deterioration. Univariate lesion analysis revealed negative association between lesions in the default mode network and postoperative attentional scores, whereas a multivariate network approach highlighted the involvement of several large-scale functional systems in sustaining attentional processes. AwS patients exhibited more extensive supramaximal resections of non-contrast-enhanced areas, which correlated with immediate postoperative attentional deterioration. The Kaplan-Meier analysis showed significantly longer overall survival for AwS patients with isocitrate dehydrogenase wild-type glioblastomas (mean days = 887.73) compared with AsS patients (mean days = 553.71; P < .05). CONCLUSION: Although AwS enables a more extensive resection and thus an improved oncological outcome with longer overall survival rate, it also leads to higher transient postoperative decline in attentional performance. These results emphasize the need for careful patient selection, especially for lesions that involve anterior anatomical regions of the left default mode network. Future developments of standardized, reliable, and quantitative intraoperative monitoring of attention may further optimize surgical outcomes.

div.head: P
div.p: rognosis of brain tumors varies widely depending on histology and biomolecular patterns 1,2 but generally remains poor for grade IV gliomas, with a median survival of 10 to 15 months. 1,[3][4][5] Moreover, patients with gliomas frequently exhibit impaired neuropsychological profiles, [6][7][8][9][10][11] because of the tumor itself or treatment (ie, surgery and/or radiotherapy and chemotherapy). [12][13][14] Awake surgery (AwS) is therefore growingly adopted for both low-grade and high-grade gliomas (LGGs and HGGs, respectively), maximizing the extent of resection (EOR) and minimizing the risks of permanent deficits. [15][16][17][18][19][20][21] However, not all patients can undergo AwS and not all cognitive functions can be monitored during surgery, [22][23][24][25] such as attention.

Attention-defined as the "cognitive processes that enable the selection of, focus on, and sustained processing of information" 26 -is of particular interest because its interdependence with other cognitive domains and functions, especially the executive system, 27 may have significant and massive implications on patients' quality of life and on personal and professional activities.

Nevertheless, this crucial cognitive domain is not routinely monitored during AwS. In fact, to date, there is only one protocol for working memory, 28 which provides an incomplete picture, given the inherent and essential nature of the complex framework supporting attentional abilities: whole-brain, highly distributed, multi-interactive, and multimodal. [29][30][31][32] Moreover, contradictory results on postoperative changes in attention are reported in the literature, with improvements 7,33,34 or impairments after surgery. 8,[35][36][37][38] A more detailed understanding of mechanisms that influence the attentional domain is therefore crucial.

To this end, (1) we compared the attentional performance of patients with brain gliomas, who underwent either asleep surgery (AsS) or AwS; (2) we compared demographical and clinical data to explain and predict the outcome of attention abilities after surgery;

(3) we analyzed oncological and survival outcomes of patients of AwS and AsS; and (4) we combined surgical resections with a functional resting-state MRI (rs-fMRI) atlas 39 and with normative rs-fMRI data, 40 providing new insights into the potential prediction of clinical outcomes.

div.head: METHODS Population
div.p: A series of 64 consecutive patients (n = 64, 42 men, mean age 53.3 years, SD = ±13.5) were included in the study (62 right-handed, 1 left-handed, 1 ambidextrous, according to the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory Test 41 ). Patients underwent awake (54.7%) or asleep (45.3%) surgery. Selection criteria are the following: no previous brain surgery, availability of presurgery and postsurgery MRI images, availability of neuropsychological assessment, and tumor gross-total resection. Regardless of tumor volume or location, AwS was proposed mainly based on patients' clinical, cognitive, and psychological status 42 (patients with good cooperative performance, no severe deficits in executive/language domains or anxiety disorders, [42][43][44] no anesthesiological contraindications 45 ). Demographic and clinical characteristics are presented in Table 1 and reported in Supplemental Digital Content 1 (http://links.lww.com/NEU/E857) with detailed inclusion criteria. This study was conducted according to the ethical standards of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Hospital Ethics Committee (Approval ID A734), for which patients gave their informed consent.

div.head: Neuropsychological Assessment
div.p: Each patient underwent a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment 20,[34][35][36]46 of every cognitive domain 1 week before surgery ("pre"), 1 week after surgery ("post"), and 1 month after surgery ("follow-up"; FU). 20,35,36 Adjuvant treatments (ie, radio-and chemotherapy) for HGG were started within 6 weeks after surgery according to established neurooncological guidelines. 47 In this study that includes both LGG and HGG, we analyzed the 1-month FU, which was therefore collected before starting other therapies, to avoid potential negative effects on cognitive abilities. Furthermore, we only considered two attentional tasks as validated in the Italian population. 48,49 Description of both tests is reported in Supplemental Digital Content 2 (http://links.lww.com/NEU/E858).
• Attentional matrices assess selective attention, 49

div.head: MRI Acquisition and Lesion Segmentation
div.p: The standard MRI evaluation protocol for glioma surgery includes the acquisition of structural, functional, and diffusion images. Details for magnetic resonance acquisition and lesion segmentation are reported in Supplemental Digital Content 3 (http://links.lww.com/NEU/E859). Lesion segmentation was performed manually on the preoperative contrast-enhanced (CE) T1 and T2/Fluid Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR) images to define CE tumor volume and non-CE volume and on the early postoperative CE T1 and T2/FLAIR images acquired 24 hours after surgery to isolate the surgical cavity and non-CE residual volume. Figure 1 shows the distribution of surgical cavities. The lesion segmentation and the calculation of EOR were performed by an expert neurosurgeon blind to the patients' surgical group (AwS or AsS) and to the purpose of this study.

div.head: Region of Interest-Based Lesion Symptom Mapping Functional Lesion Analysis
div.p: RLSM 50 analysis was performed using NiiStat Toolbox for MATLAB (https://www.nitrc.org/projects/niistat/). 51,52 This analysis was performed using the Schaefer atlas, which takes into account 1000 parcels for 7 brain functional networks derived from rs-fMRI. 39 Specifications of region of interest-based lesion symptom mapping (RLSM) method are reported in Supplemental Digital Content 4 (http://links.lww.com/ NEU/E860).

div.head: Lesion Network Mapping Analysis
div.p: Recent evidence 53 suggests that standard univariate RLSM analysis may heavily underestimate the neural substrate associated with the emergence of specific behavioral deficits. To provide a more comprehensive description of the connectional landscape subtending attention, a lesion network mapping (LNM) analysis was performed, 40 with the same procedure outlined in Coletta et al 54 . Specifications of this analysis are reported in Supplemental Digital Content 5 (http://links.lww.com/NEU/E861).

div.head: Surgical Procedure
div.p: Surgical resections were supported by a neuronavigation system that integrates structural images with tractography reconstructions of the critical white-matter pathways. During AwS, cortical and subcortical functional mapping was performed using a bipolar probe and direct electrical stimulation (60 Hz, 1 ms, 2-4 ranging mA) as previously described. [15][16][17][19][20][21][22] Specifications of awake monitoring are reported in Supplemental Digital Content 6 (http://links.lww.com/NEU/E862). During AwS, it is possible to map or monitor specific functions, 20,22,28 improving the EOR. 20,[55][56][57] However, some specific functions may only be clinically monitored: attentive functions were monitored indirectly during intraoperative neuropsychological testing through dual tasks (arm movement simultaneously performed with another cognitive task) 58,59 and assessment of executive functions by clinical observation and Stroop test. 60 Indeed, actually there are no established tools to monitor attentional functions. For AwS, tumor resection stopped when functional responses were elicited on different cognitive functions at cortical and subcortical stimulation, whereas for AsS, the resection stopped after the complete resection of the enhancing area and until reaching the reconstructions of the subcortical connections nearby the lesion.

div.head: Statistical Analysis
div.p: The analyses were conducted using SPSS v29.0, with significance level set at P < .05. Given the non-normal distribution (Shapiro-Wilk test <0.05), nonparametric analyses were performed. A binomial proportion test assessed demographical and clinical distributions. Friedman repeated-measures Analysis Of Variance (ANOVAs) were conducted for both tests, adjusted for age and education, 61 with preoperative, postoperative, and FU scores as factors. Post hoc analyses were performed using the paired Wilcoxon rank t-test. To quantify attentional decline after tumor resection, a delta (Δ) between the postoperative and preoperative scores (postoperative-preoperative) was calculated for both tests. Univariate linear regression examined the predictive effects of demographical and clinical characteristics on attentional decline. The EOR was calculated by comparing AsS and AwS using the nonparametric Mann-Whitney U test for independent samples. A two-tailed Spearman correlation assessed the relationship between EOR and Δ scores. RLSM was performed with a permutation threshold (10 000 permutations) to control for multiple comparisons, 62 using lesion volume as the regression coefficient. 62,63 Factors influencing overall survival (OS) were assessed using a univariate Cox proportional hazard regression model. The Kaplan-Meier method with log-rank test assessed the difference in OS between AwS and AsS. 64 Considering the different glioma types in our cohort, OS analyses were performed only in patients with isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) wild-type glioblastoma (ie, grade 4 tumor without IDH mutation). 2 95% CI, effect size (r) for significant results, and hazard ratio were reported for all analyses.

div.head: Demographical and Clinical Data
div.p: Our cohort was statistically unbalanced for HGG/LGG ratio (P < .001), IDH mutations (P < .001), methylated-DNA-proteincysteine methyltransferase (MGMT) methylation (P < .01), and sex (P < .05). However, none of these characteristics influenced patients' attentional decline, as shown below. All results, including 95% CI, are reported in Table 1.

div.head: Attentional Scores Outcome
div.p: Friedman ANOVA showed a significant difference in attentional matrices (P < .01), with lower postoperative scores (mean accuracy = 68.5%, P < .05) compared with preoperative assessment (mean accuracy = 71.5%). FU scores showed an improvement (mean accuracy = 75%) compared with postoperative scores (P < .01). A similar result was observed for the TMT-A (P < .01), with worse postoperative scores (mean seconds = 48.2) compared with preoperative ones (mean seconds = 8.2, P < .01). A Mann-Whitney U test was performed to compare neuropsychological scores of preoperative, postoperative, and FU separately by type of surgery: A significant difference emerged at the preoperative level, with higher baseline scores in the AwS group compared with the AsS group for both attentional matrices (P < .05) and TMT-A (P < .05). The results are reported in Supplemental Digital Content 8 (http://links.lww.com/NEU/ E864) and Figure 2C, D.

div.head: Factors Influencing Transitory Attentional Decline
div.p: We quantified the reduction in attentional scores after surgery using a Δ: patients had on average a À 3.08% (SD = ±12.04%) reduction in stimuli detection at the attentional matrices test (Δ AM ) and an increase of +10.1 seconds (SD = ±25.7) for completing the TMT-A (Δ TMT-A ). There were no predictive effects of age, sex, tumor site or grade, IDH mutation, MGMT methylation, and tumor location on Δ AM and Δ TMT-A (all Ps > 0.136). Interestingly, AsS or AwS was the only predictor for attentional decline after surgery (Δ AM P < .05; Δ TMT-A P < .01): Indeed, patients undergoing AwS showed a higher decrease of attentional scores for both Δ AM ( À 6.09%) and Δ TMT-A (+17.77 seconds) compared with AsS (+0.6% and +0.76 seconds, respectively). All results are reported in Table 3.

div.head: Non-CE EOR and Its Relationship With Postoperative Attentional Worsening
div.p: Although gross-total resection was achieved in all patients, Mann-Whitney U test determined that AwS allowed maximal supratotal resection of the non-CE area (mean 68.9%, SD = ±31.5%) compared with AsS (mean 42.7%, SD = ±33.5%; Z = À 3.21, P < .01, r = À 0.401). A two-tailed Spearman correlation confirmed a significant association between non-CE EOR and attention worsening, with a negative correlation for Δ AM and a positive correlation with Δ TMT-A (all Ps < 0.05). As for control, we tested for similar results with preoperative CE and non-CE tumor volume, using postoperative surgical cavity and hyperintensity residual: importantly, no significant correlation emerged (all Ps > 0.08). The results are reported in Supplemental Digital Content 9 (http://links.lww.com/NEU/ E865). Logistic regression showed that over 61% of non-CE EOR, there was a significantly attentional decline. The results are reported in Supplemental Digital Content 10 (http://links. lww.com/NEU/E866) and Supplemental Digital Content 11 (http://links.lww.com/NEU/E867).

div.head: RLSM Functional Lesion Analysis
div.p: The RLSM showed a significant negative association between lesions affecting the default mode network (DMN), particularly in the left prefrontal area, and postoperative attentional matrices scores (Z = À 2.94, P < .05 after permutation correction) (Figure 3A). No significant negative Z-scores were found for the postoperative TMT-A scores, neither for Δ AM nor for Δ TMT-A .

div.head: LNM Analysis
div.p: The LNM analysis revealed the involvement of a predominantly left-lateralized set of networks sustaining attentional processes. Of the 2918 voxels surviving the procedure and the selected threshold, 8.6% localized with somatomotor regions, 16.8% with the dorsal attention network, 56.9% with the ventral attention network, 15.6% with the frontoparietal network, and 1.9% with the DMN (Figure 3B).

div.head: Factors Influencing OS
div.p: From our original cohort, we separated 34 patients with IDH wild-type glioblastoma. Type of surgery (P < .05) and postoperative non-CE residual (P < .05) emerged as factors that could influence OS. Complete results are reported in Supplemental Digital Content 12 (http://links.lww.com/NEU/ E868). Non-CE residual was significantly lower in the AwS group (mean = 13.42 cc) compared with the AsS group (mean = 43.07 cc; Z = À 2.32, P < .05). In addition, the Kaplan-Meier curve with log-rank test showed significantly longer OS rate for patients in the AwS group (mean days = 887.73; median days = 572; range 290-1893 days) compared with AsS (mean days = 553.71; median days = 440; range 175-1470 days P < .05). Full results are reported in Figure 4 and Table 4. Finally, Cox regression analysis showed that a non-CE residual volume <40 cc

div.head: DISCUSSION
div.p: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first retrospective analysis of the multiple variables that may influence the modulation of attentional performance after surgery, comparing 2 different surgical techniques (awake/asleep) and considering their different effects on the EOR and OS. Moreover, we compared the fluctuations in attentional performance considering the anatomofunctional substrate using consolidated rs-fMRI approaches.

div.head: Cognitive Outcome
div.p: In our cohort, a significant decline in attentional abilities was observed 1 week after surgery, which returned to preoperative levels after 1 month. Although previous studies documented cognitive fluctuations after brain surgery, 19,36,65,66 our findings are unique considering the comparison of AwS and AsS in a mixed series of brain gliomas, without confounding factors such as adjuvant treatments 47 that largely impair cognition. 67,68 Considering all clinical variables (AsS or AwS, tumor grade, IDH mutation, MGMT status, laterality, and sex), AwS emerged as the only independent predictor of transient postoperative attentional impairment. A finer analysis showed that patients in the AwS group had a greater and significant decrease of attention immediately after surgery, with performance at 1 month comparable with preoperative performance. Conversely, the AsS group showed stable attention after surgery and an improvement 1 month after surgery for the attentional matrices. Interestingly, this result was observed only for patients of AwS, despite patients of AsS were submitted to longer general anesthesia which might itself cause fluctuations in the early postoperative outcome. 69 Moreover, despite similar attentional performance at both the 1-week and 1-month FU emerged, the preoperative assessments indicated that AwS patients had better attentional scores. This result is similar to data previously described 20 and reflects appropriate selection for AwS. Indeed, patients eligible for AwS must be cooperative, and severe deficits in attention and executive functions are exclusion criteria for this technique. 37,43 Therefore, as patients undergoing AwS show higher preoperative attentional performance, they are more likely to experience a transient decline postoperatively, with full recovery after 1 month. Despite this recovery (Supplemental Digital Content 8, http://links. lww.com/NEU/E864), attentional performance of AwS patients never improved with respect to the AsS patients. Therefore, patients' preoperative attentional abilities should also be considered when proposing AwS. However, the monitoring performed during AwS was enough to avoid permanent deficits. Attentional scores at 6-month and 12-month follow-up after surgery has been reported in Supplemental Digital Content 15 (http://links.lww.com/NEU/E871).

div.head: Oncological Outcome
div.p: Increasing evidence reports that a low rate of residual FLAIR is critical for improving OS in HGGs. Recently, the Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology (RANO) Resect Group (RANO RG) provided a new classification system for EOR in glioblastomas based on the volume of non-CE residuals. 70 Nevertheless, EOR beyond the CE area in HGGs, which can be considered the interface between the core of the tumor and the healthy brain tissue, 71 may result in cognitive impairment more frequently than resection within the enhancing borders of the tumor. In our cohort, transient impairments in attentional abilities correlated exclusively with the supramaximal EOR achieved with AwS, resulting in higher rate of non-CE resection (68.9%) compared with AsS (42.7%). In addition, our cohort showed that 61% of non-CE EOR is the cutoff value predicting worsening of attentional capacity after surgery. To compare our results in this context, we performed survival analyses including only patients with IDH wild-type glioblastoma 1,2 (N = 34). When patients with the same tumor and biomolecular pattern (IDH-wildtype Glioblastoma) were considered, the most important factor for predicting OS was the volume of non-CE residuals, in line with the conclusions of RANO RG. Crucially, patients who underwent AwS had significantly lower residual volume (13.42 cc) and longer OS (887.73 days) than those who underwent AsS (43.07 cc; mean survival = 553.71 days). Indepth analyses showed that a non-CE residual volume smaller than 40 cc was the threshold that predicted higher OS. These results, even if limited by the sample size and the retrospective design, suggest that AwS can lead to less non-CE residual volume and therefore to higher survival rates. Finally, we computed the rate of patients' progression-free survival, 70,72 which was higher for AwS (mean = 537; median = 322; range 114-1893 days) compared with AsS (mean = 382; median = 296; range = 98-1381 days). Therefore, the selection of AwS technique should be tailored for each patient, considering the feasibility of an accurate mapping and monitoring with neuropsychological tools and the literature recommendations already reported, and also an expectable higher rate of transient deficits and the possible benefit regarding EOR and of oncological outcome.

div.head: Anatomofunctional Insights
div.p: Importantly, the results of LNM analysis corroborate the notion that attention encompasses several large-scale functional brain systems. We observed involvement of the left ventral attention network and of the dorsal anterior insula. Our results are in line with recent evidence, 73 suggesting that the anterior insula might act as gatekeeper of executive control-and thus also attention.

Our analysis showed a significant association between a worsening in selective attention immediately after surgery and lesions involving the DMN. 39 Although the DMN is primarily associated with internal thought processes, [74][75][76] its deactivation is essential for effective external goal-directed behavior. 77,78 Moreover, lesions to DMN may cause an ineffective suppression of this network which can impair selective attention, as its suppression is necessary for adaptive disengagement 73,79,80 and in attention-demanding tasks. [77][78][79] Indeed, DMN plays a crucial role in brain longitudinal functional reorganization after surgery. 81

div.head: Limitations
div.p: The main limitations of this study are the small sample size, especially for survival analysis, and its retrospective design. In addition, patients' demographical and clinical characteristics were heterogeneous regarding sex, tumor grade, IDH mutation, and MGMT methylation. 1,2 However, none of these features proved to significantly affect postoperative attentional scores. Neuropsychological tests can be affected by cultural factors: Widely validated tests, such as the Trail Making Test, were used to minimize such biases. Finally, the restricted focus on attentional abilities gave us the possibility to reduce the number of statistical tests. Moreover, we implemented specific analyses to corroborate the robustness of the main results (Supplemental Digital Content 7, http://links.lww.com/NEU/E863). Notably, when the number of tests was increased, we carefully controlled for Type I errors with state-of-the-art approaches (10.000 permutations threshold for RLSM 62 and the threshold-free cluster enhancement approach for LNM 40 ,54 ).

div.head: CONCLUSION
div.p: Among the clinical factors considered, the only one affecting the attentional outcome was AwS. This technique allowed a larger supramaximal EOR in HGGs, resulting in a temporary impairment at 1-week FU, while improving OS. One month after surgery, attentional scores recovered in both groups. Finally, we highlighted the role of a left prefrontal region in the DMN in attentional processes, providing new insights in the definition of safe functional margin of resection for attention.
